definition: A small program that runs part of your code and checks the result without a person watching. Because it costs almost nothing to re-run, it can check old behaviour after every change.
example: A test that calls apply_discount(50.0, 10) and checks the answer is 45.0 runs in a fraction of a millisecond.

definition: The whole collection of automated tests for a project, usually run together with one command. A fast, trusted suite is what lets a team change code without fear.
example: A project's suite might hold 4,000 unit tests and 300 integration tests, all run by pytest on every change.

definition: A test that checks behaviour which used to work still works, often written when a bug is fixed so the same bug cannot quietly return. A regression is a change that breaks something that previously worked.
example: After fixing a crash on orders with quantity 0, you keep test_invoice_with_zero_quantity in the suite for good.

definition: Tests read as documentation that can be run: their names and assertions describe what the code promises, and running them shows whether the code still keeps that promise.
example: test_full_discount_is_free tells a newcomer that a 100 % discount gives a price of 0.

definition: The most widely used third-party test framework for Python. It finds test files and functions by naming convention, runs them, and reports failures with the values involved, using plain assert statements.
example: Running pytest -q in a project prints one dot per passing test and a summary such as "3 passed in 0.05s".

definition: A tool that finds tests, runs them and reports which passed and failed. pytest is the usual test runner for Python.

How a test runner finds tests without being told each one. By default pytest collects files named test_*.py or *_test.py and, inside them, functions and methods whose names start with test; configuration can change these rules.
example: A function called check_total is not collected by default, so it never runs.

definition: A common layout for a test in three visible steps: arrange (set up inputs and objects), act (call the code being tested, ideally one line) and assert (check the outcome).
example: Arrange: cart = Cart(vat_rate=0.2). Act: total = cart.total(). Assert: total == 24.00.

definition: A statement that a condition must be true at that point in the program; if it is false, the check fails. In a test it is how the result is checked, written in Python and pytest with the assert statement.
example: assert apply_discount(50.0, 10) == 45.0 fails the test if the function returns anything other than 45.0.

definition: The Python exception raised when an assert statement's condition is false. pytest catches it and reports the values that were compared.
example: assert 'a-b' == 'a_b' raises AssertionError, which pytest shows as a failed test.

definition: Testing the inputs at the edges of a valid range, and one step outside them, because off-by-one mistakes cluster there. Zero, one, empty, the maximum and the limits of a range check are typical boundary values.
example: For a rule age >= 18, test 18 (allowed) and 17 (refused), not just 30 and 10.

definition: A test that drives the whole deployed system from the outside, the way a user or client would, for example through a real browser. E2E tests are the most realistic but also the slowest, most flaky and hardest to diagnose.
example: A Playwright test opens the shop in a browser, clicks Add to basket and Checkout, and checks that "Order confirmed" appears.

definition: A guideline, popularised by Mike Cohn, to have many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few end-to-end tests. It is a heuristic about cost and speed, not a fixed ratio.
example: Google suggested a 70/20/10 split of unit, integration and E2E tests as a first guess.

definition: A test suite shaped like an upside-down pyramid: few unit tests and many slow end-to-end or manual tests. It tends to be slow, flaky and untrusted.
example: A suite that takes an hour and is re-run until it goes green is a typical ice-cream cone.

definition: Quality assurance: the work of checking that software meets its requirements, often by dedicated testers running manual or automated checks.
example: A team with manual QA scripts runs through a checklist of clicks before every release.

definition: Kent C. Dodds's alternative to the test pyramid for front-end code: static analysis at the base and most of the effort in integration tests that render components with their real children, with fewer unit and end-to-end tests.
Spotify's suggested test shape for microservices: mostly integration tests per service, few tests of internal implementation details and very few tests that need other services running.
Checking code without running it, for example with a linter or a type checker. It catches typos, type errors and style problems before any test runs.
example: A type checker reports that a function expecting an int is passed a str.

definition: The part of an application that users see and interact with, such as web pages running in a browser, as opposed to the back-end servers.

Google's classification of tests by the resources they may use. Small tests run in a single process with no sleeping or external I/O; medium tests may use several processes and localhost networking on one machine; large tests may span machines.
example: A test that starts a local server in a second process and calls it on localhost is at least medium.

definition: How much code a test exercises, from one function (narrow) to the whole system (broad). Google treats scope as separate from size, which is about the resources a test uses.

Self-contained: a hermetic test (or build) depends only on what it declares or sets up itself, with no access to shared or outside resources such as the network, so nothing outside it can change its result.
example: An in-memory filesystem created by the test is hermetic; a shared network drive is not.

definition: Always producing the same result from the same inputs. A nondeterministic test can pass or fail on the same code because of hidden inputs such as the clock, randomness or timing. (A "deterministic profiler" uses the word differently: it records every call instead of sampling.)
example: A test that reads datetime.now() is nondeterministic unless the clock is injected or frozen.

definition: A CI run in which at least one check failed (red) rather than all passing (green). Teams usually block merging while the build is red.

Input/output: a program reading or writing anything outside its own memory, such as files, the network or a terminal. I/O is slow and unpredictable compared with in-memory work, which is why small tests avoid it.
One thousandth of a second, written ms. Good unit tests take around a millisecond or less.
example: 4,000 unit tests at 2 ms each take 8 seconds.

definition: One millionth of a second, written µs. Calling a test double in memory takes microseconds, while a network call takes milliseconds.
The network name a computer uses for itself, normally the address 127.0.0.1. Traffic to localhost never leaves the machine.
example: A test HTTP server listening on localhost port 8000 is reachable only from that computer.

definition: Running inside the same operating-system process as the test, so calls are ordinary function calls in memory with no network or separate program involved. A process is one running program with its own memory.
A widely used open-source relational database server.
A 2020 book by Titus Winters, Tom Manshreck and Hyrum Wright describing Google's engineering practices, including its testing approach. It is free to read online.
A unit test that isolates the code under test from all its collaborators by replacing them with test doubles.
A unit test that lets the code use its real collaborators, as long as they are fast and in-process.

A mnemonic for good unit tests: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating and Timely, as listed in Robert C. Martin's Clean Code (2008). Tim Ottinger and Jeff Langr's version reads Isolated and Self-verifying for I and S.
Another object or function that the code under test calls on to do its job, such as a repository, a mailer or a clock.
example: An OrderService's collaborators might be a pricer, a tax calculator and a payment client.

definition: A pytest helper, used in a with block, that makes the test pass only if the block raises the given exception type (or a subclass). Its match argument also requires the error message to match a regular expression.
example: with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must be"): parse_age("-3")

definition: A pytest helper for comparing floating-point numbers within a tolerance instead of exactly. By default it allows a relative difference of 10^-6 (one part in a million) with an absolute floor of 10^-12.
example: assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3) passes.

definition: An allowed error expressed as a fraction of the expected value, so bigger expected values allow bigger absolute differences.
example: A relative tolerance of 10^-6 on an expected 1,000,000 allows a difference of 1.

definition: An allowed error expressed as a fixed amount, regardless of the size of the expected value. It matters most when the expected value is close to zero.
A pytest decorator that runs one test function once for each set of arguments in a list, reporting each case as a separate test.
example: Three (title, slug) pairs give three separately reported tests.

definition: Every combination of one value from each list. Stacking parametrize decorators produces this, so the numbers of values multiply.
example: 3 values of a and 2 values of b give 3 × 2 = 6 tests.

definition: A function marked with @pytest.fixture that provides something a test needs, such as an object, a connection or a temporary directory. A test asks for it by naming it as a parameter, and code after a yield runs as teardown.
example: A fixture named account returns Account(balance=100) for every test that lists account as a parameter.

definition: Setup prepares what a test needs before it runs; teardown cleans up afterwards, for example closing a connection or deleting a temporary file.

How long one instance of a pytest fixture lives and is shared: function scope (the default) creates it fresh for each test, module scope once per test file, and session scope once per whole run. Wider scope is faster but lets tests leak state into each other.
A built-in pytest fixture that gives each test a fresh temporary directory as a pathlib.Path object.
A built-in pytest fixture that captures what the code under test prints, so the test can check the output.
A named setting, such as DB_URL, that the operating system passes to a running program. It is a common way to configure an application without changing its code.

A warning or failure raised when nothing is actually wrong. In testing, a test that fails although the code's observable behaviour has not changed; frequent false alarms teach people to ignore failures.
example: A test that checks svc._cache breaks when the dict is swapped for lru_cache, though prices are unchanged.

definition: How code achieves its result internally, such as private attributes, helper methods or a cache's data structure, as opposed to its observable behaviour. Tests coupled to implementation details break on harmless refactors.
The functions, methods and attributes a piece of code offers for other code to use, as opposed to its private internals.
A method or attribute meant only for use inside its own class. Python marks these by convention with a leading underscore, such as _cache.
Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases: the advice to make each test readable on its own, even at the cost of some repetition, rather than hiding its details behind shared helpers.
example: make_user(age=17) shows the one value that matters to the test.

definition: Data that more than one part of a program, such as several threads, requests or tests, can read and change. It makes results depend on which code ran first, so it is a common cause of race conditions and order-dependent tests.
A test that checks more than the behaviour it is about, such as a whole 40-field response when one field matters, so it fails for many unrelated reasons.
Python's fixed-length, unchangeable sequence, written with commas and usually brackets, such as (1, "a"). Any non-empty tuple counts as true in an if or assert.
A value Python treats as true in a condition. Empty containers, 0, None and False are falsy; almost everything else, including a non-empty tuple, is truthy.
A pattern language for matching text. Python's re.search looks for the pattern anywhere in a string.
example: re.search("must be", "age must be >= 0") finds a match.

definition: The exception Python's database drivers raise when a change would break a database rule, such as inserting a duplicate value into a UNIQUE column.
The starting value for a pseudo-random number generator. The same seed always produces the same sequence of numbers, so fixing or recording it makes random tests repeatable.
example: random.Random(42) gives the same numbers on every run.

definition: A test double that is passed to fill a parameter but never actually used.
example: Passing None as a logger to a code path that never logs.

definition: A test double that returns canned answers to calls, without checking how it was called.
example: A rates service that always returns 1.17 for GBP to EUR.

definition: A stub that also records how it was called, so the test can check the calls afterwards.
example: A mailer double that records every send() call.

definition: A test double pre-programmed with the calls it expects, which fails the test if they do not happen. Informally, "mock" is often used for any test double.
example: A payment double that fails the test unless charge() is called exactly once with (card, 10).

definition: A test double with a real, working but simplified implementation that takes a shortcut, usually keeping data in memory instead of in a database. Unlike a stub it has real behaviour, such as enforcing unique emails.
example: An InMemoryUsers class that stores users in a dict and rejects a duplicate email stands in for the real database repository.

definition: The family of unit-test frameworks descended from Smalltalk's SUnit and Java's JUnit. Gerard Meszaros's book xUnit Test Patterns (2007) introduced the standard test-double names.
The part of Python's standard library for creating test doubles. Its Mock class accepts most attribute access and calls, records them and can be told what to return.
A unittest.mock class like Mock that also supports Python's magic methods, such as len() and iteration.
A Python method with double underscores either side of its name, such as __len__, that Python calls for built-in operations like len(x) or iteration.
The attribute of a unittest.mock Mock that sets what a call to it returns.
example: rates.get.return_value = 1.17

definition: The attribute of a unittest.mock Mock that makes calls raise an exception, return successive items from a list, or run a function.
example: Mock(side_effect=[TimeoutError, {"status": "paid"}]) raises first, then returns the dict.

definition: Methods and attributes of a unittest.mock Mock for checking how it was called: assert_called_once_with checks one call with given arguments, assert_not_called checks there were none, call_count counts calls and call_args_list lists them.
A unittest.mock function that temporarily replaces a named object, such as "checkout.charge", with a double while a test runs, then restores it. It must target the name where it is looked up.
The set of names a module, class or function can see and what each refers to. from payments import charge copies the name charge into the importing module's namespace.
A unittest.mock feature that builds a double copying the real object's attribute names and call signatures, so calling a method with missing or extra arguments raises TypeError.

Passing spec=SomeClass to a Mock restricts attribute lookup to names the class really has, so typos raise AttributeError; spec_set also blocks setting unknown attributes. Neither checks call arguments.
The parameters a function or method accepts: their names, order, and which are required.
example: charge(card, amount, currency) has three required parameters.

definition: Checking a result by inspecting the state after the code runs, such as reading a saved user back from a repository.
Checking a result by asserting which calls the code made to its test doubles, such as that repo.add was called once with given arguments. Also called behaviour verification.
The school of TDD (also called Detroit or Chicago school) that uses real objects where possible, doubles only awkward collaborators, and prefers state verification.
The school of TDD (also called London school) that isolates each class, replaces all its collaborators with mocks, and verifies interactions, typically working outside-in.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing platform.

An isolated environment where code or actions cannot affect real systems. Most often here: a provider's test version of its service that behaves like the real one with no real effects, such as a payment sandbox that accepts test card numbers without charging anyone.
The HTTP status code meaning Service Unavailable: the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, for example because it is overloaded or down for maintenance.

A place where two parts of a system meet, such as your code and a database, or two services. Michael Feathers also uses it for a place where behaviour can be swapped (for example by injecting a dependency) without editing the code there. Bugs that unit tests cannot see often live at seams.
An integration test that exercises only the code talking to one external thing, such as a repository class against a real database, with everything else doubled or absent.
An integration test that brings up many real services together and tests through all of them. It overlaps with end-to-end testing and shares its slowness.
Undoing all changes made in an open database transaction. Tests often open a transaction and roll it back afterwards so each test starts from a clean database; it cannot undo work already committed.
Making a database transaction's changes permanent, with the SQL command COMMIT or a driver call such as conn.commit(). After a commit, a rollback can no longer undo them.
A marker inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction.
The SQL command that quickly removes all rows from a table. Tests use it for cleanup when rollback cannot undo the changes.
SQLite's approach to column types: a declared type is only a preference, so most columns accept values of any type, and lengths such as VARCHAR(3) are not enforced.
example: SQLite stores 'GBPX' in a VARCHAR(3) column without complaint.

definition: An SQL text column type with a maximum length, such as VARCHAR(3). Postgres rejects longer values; SQLite ignores the limit.
An SQL column type for text of any length. SQLite maps VARCHAR and similar declared types to TEXT affinity.
A database rule that no two rows may have the same value in a column, such as an email address. Breaking it raises an integrity error.
An insert that updates the existing row instead if one with the same key already exists. Postgres writes it as INSERT ... ON CONFLICT.
A Postgres (and recent SQLite) clause that makes an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE return the affected rows' values.
A library, available for Python and other languages, that starts real services such as Postgres in throwaway Docker containers from test code and removes them afterwards.
A popular tool for packaging an application with everything it needs and running it in an isolated container.
Held in RAM (the computer's main working memory) rather than on disk or across a network: fast to reach, but normally lost when the program ends unless it is saved somewhere.
example: SQLite's ":memory:" database lives only in RAM.

definition: A local server that returns canned HTTP responses, so a real HTTP client can be tested without the real service.
A popular tool for running a stub HTTP server that returns configured responses to matching requests.
A Python library that intercepts requests made with the httpx client inside the same process and returns canned responses; no real network traffic happens.
Code that sends HTTP requests to a server and handles its responses.
A named field sent with an HTTP request or response, such as Content-Type, carrying extra information about the message.
A browser automation tool, with a Python version, that drives real browsers for end-to-end tests. Its expect assertions retry until a condition holds or a timeout passes.
A long-established tool for automating web browsers, widely used for end-to-end tests.
A copy of the production setup used to try out changes before they reach real users.
A temporary copy of the system created for one branch or test run and thrown away afterwards, so tests do not share an environment with other teams.
The language that sets how web pages look. CSS selectors pick elements by tag, class or position, and change whenever a page is restyled.
A query language for selecting parts of an HTML or XML document by their position in the element tree.
An expression that tells a browser-testing tool which page element to act on, such as a button's role and name, a test id or a CSS path.
An attribute added to a page element only so tests can find it reliably, such as data-testid="pay".
A class that wraps one page of a user interface and offers methods such as pay_with(card), so tests do not depend directly on the page's structure.

A test that checks the agreement between two pieces of software, such as the requests a consumer sends and the response fields it relies on, against the real provider, without deploying both together.
In contract testing, the service that calls an API. Its tests record which requests it sends and which response fields it needs.
In contract testing, the service that offers an API. Its CI replays consumers' contracts against its real code.
A contract written from what consumers actually use, so the provider may change anything no consumer depends on.
A contract the provider publishes, such as an OpenAPI or protobuf schema, against which consumers are checked. It shows the shape of the API but not which fields any consumer needs.
An open-source tool for consumer-driven contract testing. Consumer tests run against a Pact mock server and generate a pact file that the provider then verifies.

A server that stores pact files from every consumer and records verification results, so providers can fetch relevant contracts and teams can check compatibility before deploying. PactFlow is a hosted commercial version of it.
A Pact Broker command that checks whether a version of a service has been verified as compatible with the versions of its consumers or providers in a given environment.
The HTTP method for fetching a resource without changing it.
example: GET /users/42 asks for user 42.

definition: The three-digit number in an HTTP response that says how the request went, such as 200 (OK) or 503 (Service Unavailable).
Test-driven development: writing a small failing test before the code that makes it pass, then tidying up, in a short repeated cycle. Described by Kent Beck in 2002.
The TDD cycle: write a failing test (red), write the simplest code that passes it (green), then clean up with all tests passing (refactor).

term: Fake it till you make it
definition: A TDD tactic from Kent Beck: first make a test pass with the simplest possible code, even a hard-coded answer, then let further tests force the real logic.
example: parse_duration returning 3600 for every input passes the first test.

definition: In TDD, adding a second, different example so that a hard-coded answer can no longer pass, pushing the code towards a general solution.
An error case through code, such as bad input or a failed call, as opposed to the happy path where nothing goes wrong.
A test that checks a whole feature meets its requirements from the user's or customer's point of view.
A TDD style that starts with a failing acceptance test for a whole feature and then builds the inner pieces with unit-level TDD, often doubling collaborators not yet written.
A quick experimental piece of code written to learn how to solve a problem, then thrown away and rebuilt properly.
Testing by stating a rule that must hold for all valid inputs and letting a library generate many inputs to try to break it, instead of choosing each example by hand.
An ordinary test that checks specific inputs and outputs chosen by the author.
The original property-based testing library, for Haskell, by Koen Claessen and John Hughes (2000).
A purely functional programming language.
The main property-based testing library for Python. It generates inputs from strategies, shrinks failing ones and saves them in an example database.
An object in Hypothesis that describes how to generate values, such as st.integers() or st.lists(st.text()).
The Hypothesis decorator that turns a test into a property test, supplying generated values for its arguments from the strategies given.
A Hypothesis decorator that adds a fixed input which always runs alongside the generated ones; used to pin known tricky cases.
The Hypothesis setting for how many satisfying examples to try in a successful run; default 100.
Where Hypothesis stores failing examples (by default in a local .hypothesis/ directory) so they are replayed first on later runs.

What a property-based testing library does after finding a failing input: repeatedly tries simpler versions (shorter lists, smaller numbers) and keeps any that still fail, to report a small counterexample. It does not guarantee the smallest possible one.
example: A failure on a=[-91, 3, 3, 17], b=[3, 40] shrinks to a=[0], b=[0].

definition: A specific input for which a claimed rule fails.
A property that converting a value and converting it back gives the original, such as decode(encode(x)) == x.
A trusted way to work out the right answer for a test. In property-based testing, a simple, obviously correct implementation checks a fast or clever one.
example: sorted(a + b) acts as the oracle for a hand-written merge.

definition: The property of a function that applying it twice gives the same result as applying it once: f(f(x)) = f(x).
example: Trimming spaces from a string is idempotent.

definition: Testing by checking how outputs should relate when the input is changed in a known way, useful when the exact right answer is hard to know.
example: Adding a filter to a search should never return more results.

definition: A simple compression method that stores each run of repeated characters as a count followed by the character.
example: "aaab" becomes "3a1b".

definition: Property-based testing that generates sequences of operations against a system and a simple model of it, checking they agree after each step.
Python's standard functions for converting values to JSON text (dumps) and back (loads).
A special floating-point value meaning Not a Number, produced by undefined results such as 0.0/0.0 in some languages. NaN is not equal to anything, even itself.
A test that can both pass and fail on the same code without any change. Causes include timing, test order, the clock, randomness, shared resources and real race conditions.
A test whose result depends on which other tests ran before it, usually because they share state.
A pytest plugin that shuffles test order on every run and reseeds random generators, printing the seed so a failing order can be replayed.
A pytest plugin that runs tests in several processes in parallel, for example with pytest -n 4.
A pytest plugin that automatically re-runs failing tests a set number of times.
A pytest plugin that measures code coverage with coverage.py while the tests run.
Python libraries (freezegun and time-machine) that make code see a fixed or controlled current time during a test.
Daylight saving time: moving clocks forward in summer, which creates days with 23 or 25 hours and a source of time-related bugs.
A temporary network port the operating system picks automatically; asking to listen on port 0 gets a free one, so parallel tests do not clash.
Moving a flaky test out of the suite that blocks merging while it is fixed, usually with an owner and deadline, and still running it to collect data.
The underlying reason a problem happens, as opposed to its symptoms.
A measure of which parts of the code ran while the tests ran. It shows untested code but not whether the results were checked.
The standard Python tool for measuring code coverage, including branch coverage with the --branch option.
The share of executable statements that ran at least once during the tests.
The share of possible branch outcomes (such as the true and false sides of each if) that the tests took.
One of the ways a decision in code can go: an if has two outcomes, true (the branch is taken) and false. Branch coverage counts which outcomes the tests produced.
example: if total >= 50 has two branch outcomes: total is at least 50, or it is not.

definition: One complete route that execution takes through a piece of code from entry to exit, fixed by which way each decision goes. Different inputs can follow different paths, and independent decisions multiply the number of possible paths.
example: Two independent if statements give four execution paths: true-true, true-false, false-true and false-false.

definition: Exercising every distinct route through a piece of code from entry to exit. The number of paths can grow exponentially with independent decisions, so full path coverage is often infeasible.
Stopping the evaluation of an expression as soon as its result is known. In Python's a and b, b is skipped if a is false; in a or b, b is skipped if a is true.
The observation that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure, because people optimise the number rather than what it was meant to show.
A method whose only job is to return the value of an attribute. Tests of trivial getters raise coverage without checking much.
Another engineer reading and commenting on a change before it is merged.
Measuring test strength by making many small deliberate changes (mutants) to the code and checking whether the tests fail for each.
A copy of the code with one small deliberate change, such as >= turned into >. If a test fails, the mutant is killed; if all tests pass, it survived.
A mutant for which all tests still pass. It may reveal a missing test, be an equivalent mutant, or concern behaviour outside the contract.

The percentage of mutants the tests killed. Strictly it is killed mutants divided by killable (non-equivalent) mutants, but tools cannot detect most equivalent mutants, so the score they report often divides by all generated mutants.
A mutant whose behaviour is indistinguishable from the original, so no test can kill it. Deciding equivalence is undecidable in general.
Describes a question no algorithm can answer correctly for every possible input.
Google's term for code unlikely to matter for testing, such as logging calls, which its mutation system skips.
A mutation testing tool for Python.
A mutation testing tool for Python (installed as the cosmic-ray package).
A mutation testing tool for Java and other JVM languages.
A mutation testing framework for JavaScript/TypeScript, C# and Scala.
An operation that happens completely or not at all, with no other thread able to see it half done.
Reading a value, changing it and writing it back. Without synchronisation, two threads doing it at once can lose an update.
Floating-point numbers have both +0.0 and -0.0; they compare equal but can be told apart, for example by their sign.
